chapter.title: Keeping the keys: saving every good version with Git and GitHub

cards.body:
Your app worked perfectly at 4pm. At 6pm it's a blank white page. Can you get 4pm back?

Think of each working version as a photo of the house plus a spare key. Git keeps those in a drawer at home, and GitHub keeps copies in a safe across town. **The builder can knock down walls, but you keep the keys to every version that worked.**
cards.simpler:
Your app worked fine at 4pm. By 6pm it shows only a blank white page. Can you get the 4pm version back?

Picture each working version as a photo of your house plus a spare key. Git keeps these in a drawer at home. GitHub keeps copies in a safe across town. **The builder can knock down walls, but you keep the keys to every version that worked.**

cards.prompt: Priya's habit tracker worked last night. This morning Claude added a dark mode, and now every button has vanished. What gets last night's version back fastest?

options.text: Ask Claude to rebuild the whole app from scratch
Go back to a save point made last night, while it worked
Keep asking Claude to fix the buttons until they reappear

whyNot.a: That's starting over, not going back. You'd get a new app, not last night's working one.
whyNot.c: That's fixing forward, not going back. It might work, or it might take ten more tries and break something else.

cards.reteach: A save point is a frozen copy of every file at one moment. If you made one while the app worked, getting back to it takes one request. If you didn't, all you can do is patch the new mess.

cards.title: Save, then upload
cards.body:
*Git* is a save-point system that lives inside your project folder. Each save point is called a *commit*: a snapshot of every file, plus a short note saying what works. It's like a dated photo of the house after each room is finished.

*GitHub* is a website that keeps a copy of those commits online. Sending them there is called a *push*, which just means upload.

You don't type any of this yourself. **You tell Claude in plain English: “commit this as ‘score counter works’”, then “push to GitHub”.** The first push asks you to sign in to GitHub once.
cards.simpler:
Git is a save-point tool inside your project folder. Each save point is a commit: a copy of every file at that moment, plus a short note on what works. It's like a dated photo of the house.

GitHub is a website that keeps your commits online. Sending them there is a push, which means upload.

You type no commands. **You tell Claude: “commit this as ‘score counter works’”, then “push to GitHub”.** The first push asks you to sign in once.

cards.title: Sam's Tuesday
cards.body: Sam's tip calculator splits a dinner bill between 4 people, and on Monday at 9pm it works. Sam types: “commit this as ‘tip split works for 4 people’ and push it.” On Tuesday Sam asks for a currency picker, and the page goes blank. Sam types: **“go back to the last commit.”** Monday's calculator is back within a minute. The currency picker is gone, and so is the blank page, which is exactly the trade you want.
cards.simpler: Sam built a tip calculator that splits a dinner bill between 4 people. On Monday at 9pm it works, so Sam types: “commit this as ‘tip split works for 4 people’ and push it.” On Tuesday Sam asks for a currency picker, and the page goes blank. Sam types: **“go back to the last commit.”** Within a minute, Monday's calculator is back. The currency picker is gone, but so is the blank page. That's the trade you want.

cards.prompt: Ana asked Claude to add a ‘delete task’ button to her to-do app. When should she say “commit this”?

options.text: Right after Claude says it's done, before trying it
After clicking the button a few times and watching tasks disappear properly
On Friday, once the whole week's changes are in

whyNot.a: That's saving a promise, not a working version. If the button is broken, the save point is broken too.
whyNot.c: That's one save point for five days instead of one per working step. Going back would wipe out the whole week.

cards.reteach: A commit is only as good as what's inside it. Test first, so the save point you'd come back to actually works. Then save straight away, before the next change.

cards.title: Two copies, and why you need both
cards.body:
A commit lives on your laptop. Spill coffee on the laptop and every save point goes with it. A push copies them to GitHub, the safe across town, so a new computer can download your whole project again.

You'd think lots of saves would make a mess. It's the opposite: **each commit is an undo you can use any day, not just the most recent one.** Ask Claude “show me my last 5 commits” and you get a list of notes like ‘login works’ and ‘colours fixed’.

That's why the note matters. A note that just says ‘update’ tells future-you nothing.
cards.simpler:
A commit lives on your laptop. Spill coffee on it and every save point is gone. A push copies them to GitHub, the safe across town, so a new computer can download your project again.

Many saves don't make a mess. **Each commit is an undo you can use any day, not just the latest one.** Ask Claude “show me my last 5 commits” and you'll see notes like ‘login works’.

That's why notes matter. ‘Update’ tells future-you nothing.

cards.body: Leo's quiz app half-worked at 11pm, and Leo committed it anyway as ‘nearly done’. Two days later something broke. Leo went back to that save point, and the half-broken quiz came back with it. **A save point is only as good as what was working when you made it.** Before you say “commit”, click through the app once yourself.
cards.simpler: At 11pm, Leo's quiz app only half worked, but Leo saved it anyway with the note ‘nearly done’. Two days later something broke. Leo went back to that save point, and the half-broken quiz came back with it. **A save point is only as good as what worked when you made it.** So before you say “commit”, click through your app once yourself.

cards.prompt: Three things are left over from Thursday. Which one can actually bring back Thursday's working app?

options.text: Your chat with Claude from Thursday, scrolled back up
A commit called ‘wip’, made halfway through a change and never pushed
A commit called ‘photo upload works’, made after testing and pushed to GitHub

whyNot.a: That's a record of what you asked for, not a copy of the files. The files have changed since then.
whyNot.b: That's a save of something unfinished, not a working version, and it lives on only one laptop.

cards.reteach: To go back, you need three things: a real save point (a commit), made while the app worked, and stored somewhere safe (GitHub). A chat log has none of these. A half-done save has only the first.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Git takes a snapshot of your project each time you say “commit”, and GitHub keeps a copy online when you say “push”. **Test it, commit it, push it**, and yesterday's working app is always one sentence away.

Tomorrow: why asking for one feature beats asking for five at once.
cards.simpler:
Each time you say “commit”, Git takes a snapshot of your project. When you say “push”, GitHub keeps a copy online. **Test it, commit it, push it**, and yesterday's working app is always one sentence away.

Tomorrow: why asking for one feature beats asking for five at once.

cards.body: Open Claude Code in your project folder and type: “Is this folder using Git yet? If not, set it up and commit everything as ‘first working version’.” Then ask it to show you that commit.
cards.simpler: Open Claude Code in your project folder. Then type this: **“Is this folder using Git yet? If not, set it up and commit everything as ‘first working version’.”** When it's done, ask Claude to show you that commit. That's your very first save point, and it's the one you can come back to if something breaks.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now save a working version, upload it to GitHub, and bring it back when a new change breaks things.
